# Epigraph Concordance

!!! quote "On the form"
    The epigraphs here are categorised by writer rather than by quotation,
    because there are many, and one writer may hold more than one
    *epigraphorism©*. See [Epigraphorism©](lexicon.md#epigraphorism) in the
    Lexicon. — *J. L. Roapes*

**17 epigraphs · 13 writers.** Generated from the collected drafts — do not edit by hand; edit the source and rebuild. Every entry has a permanent anchor, so any line here can be linked from anywhere else on the site.

---

## Honoré de Balzac { #honore-de-balzac }

> "How many horrible and beautiful things!"

<cite id="honore-de-balzac-how-many-horrible-and-beautiful">Facino Cane</cite>



## Roland Barthes { #roland-barthes }

> "Better the illusions of subjectivity than the impostures of objectivity. Better the Imaginary of the subject than its censorship."

<cite id="roland-barthes-better-the-illusions-of-subjecti">The Preparation of the Novel (Session of December 2, 1978)</cite>


> "...despite the fact that they keep happening, these ‘catastrophes’ are never planned for: the weather only exists after the event, as a discourse of irresponsibility."

<cite id="roland-barthes-despite-the-fact-that-they-ke">The Preparation of the Novel (Session of January 20, 1979)</cite>



## Jorge Luis Borges { #jorge-luis-borges }

> "We could not deceive one another, and that makes conversation hard."

<cite id="jorge-luis-borges-we-could-not-deceive-one-another">“The Other” from The Book of Sand (1975)</cite>



## Edward Dahlberg { #edward-dahlberg }

> "Only those who know the ocean ponder death as they behold it, whereas those bound closely to the ground are more sensual."

<cite id="edward-dahlberg-only-those-who-know-the-ocean-po">Because I Was Flesh (19XX)</cite>



## Brian Dillon { #brian-dillon }

> "Only poets come close."

<cite id="brian-dillon-only-poets-come-close">“How How How What What What How—When” Suppose a Sentence (2020)</cite>



## Witold Gombrowicz { #witold-gombrowicz }

> "He intended nothing at all because he wrote the way a child pees against a tree, in order to relieve himself."

<cite id="witold-gombrowicz-he-intended-nothing-at-all-becau">Diary: Volume One (1953)</cite>



## Kenneth Koch { #kenneth-koch }

> "Isn’t this history, and aren’t we a couple of ruins"

<cite id="kenneth-koch-isnt-this-history-and-arent-w">“In Love with You” (First published in Apr. 1955, Poetry Magazine )</cite>



## Henry Miller { #henry-miller }

> "Nothing, on deep analysis, proves to be what it seems or purports to be. Man continues to hunger."

<cite id="henry-miller-nothing-on-deep-analysis-prove">The Books in my Life (1969)</cite>


> "Never was the fear of life so rampant. The fear of life has replaced the fear of death."

<cite id="henry-miller-never-was-the-fear-of-life-so-ra">The Books in my Life (1969)</cite>



## Oscar Milosz { #oscar-milosz }

> "You, sad, sad sound of rain on the rain"

<cite id="oscar-milosz-you-sad-sad-sound-of-rain-on-t">“Les Terrains vagues” Andramandoni (1918)</cite>



## Marianne Moore { #marianne-moore }

> "Dürer would have seen a reason for living in a town like this, with eight stranded whales to look at; with the sweet sea air coming into your house"

<cite id="marianne-moore-durer-would-have-seen-a-reason-f">“The Steeple-Jack” from Selected Poems (1935)</cite>



## Fernando Pessoa { #fernando-pessoa }

> "Living life falsely and in dreams is still living life."

<cite id="fernando-pessoa-living-life-falsely-and-in-dream">The Book of Disquiet, Entry 49</cite>



## Susan Sontag { #susan-sontag }

> "I took a trip to see the beautiful things."

<cite id="susan-sontag-i-took-a-trip-to-see-the-beautif">“Unguided Tour” The New Yorker (Oct. 1977)</cite>
<br><small>— By way of Brian Dillon’s “Suppose a Sentence”</small>



## Natsume Sōseki { #natsume-soseki }

> "However you look at it, the human world is not an easy place to live."

<cite id="natsume-soseki-however-you-look-at-it-the-huma">Kusamakura (1906)</cite>


> "The early Zen priest Daie is said to have suffered greatly from the fact that even the enlightened mind, which has mastered the illusion of reality, is still troubled by dreams of the vulgar world."

<cite id="natsume-soseki-the-early-zen-priest-daie-is-sai">Kusamakura (1906)</cite>


> "The main path has become indistinguishable among the numerous tracks that meet and part and intersect. All are a path of some sort, and none is the path itself."

<cite id="natsume-soseki-the-main-path-has-become-indisti">Kusamakura (1906)</cite>
